newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FOCUS - Mkts reacted appropriately to G7 - Tietmeyer.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Mkts reacted appropriately to G7 - Tietmeyer.

text.p: Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said on Monday that financial markets had reacted appropriately to signals from the Group of Seven (G7) industrialised countries that the dollar had risen far enough.

The dollar slipped against major currencies in Asian trading after the meeting of G7 finance ministers and central bankers in Berlin on Saturday, but recovered in Europe to approach Friday's levels in calm trading.
Speaking after the regular monthly meeting of central bank governors from the broader Group of 10 (G10), Tietmeyer told reporters that he had briefed his colleagues on the Berlin meeting.
"I informed them about the consensus reached in Berlin on the exchange-rate side," he said at the Bank for International Settlements in Basle.

Asked whether he was happy with markets' reaction to the G7 statement, he said: "Until now we saw the markets reacted in an appropriate way. The message sent from Berlin seems to be understood by the markets."

In their statement, the G7 nations -- Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States -- signalled their desire for stability in the foreign exchange markets by saying their currencies were no longer misaligned in a big way.
The G10 -- which actually includes 11 countries -- comprises the G7 plus Belgium, the Netherlands, Sweden and Switzerland.
In general, Tietmeyer gave an upbeat assessment of the global economic outlook for growth and inflation.
"The economic situation worldwide is in a positive way as far as growth and inflation are concerned," he told reporters.
G10 central bankers also discussed the need for long-term structural reform to address "relatively high" unemployment in Europe, said Tietmeyer, who chairs the group.

They discussed structural reforms "because there is a clear understanding most unemployment is of a structural nature", he said, citing inflexible labour markets as one area that needed to be changed.
Tietmeyer said he hoped economic growth would help solve some of the unemployment problems, but at the same time stressed that structural issues had to be addressed in a convincing way.

The G10 meeting also focused on the impact of budget consolidation as European Union countries strive to meet the strict convergence criteria necessary to qualify for the single currency due to start in 1999.
"I think it is necessary to continue consolidation of budgets. It is important there are substantial and lasting improvements," Tietmeyer said.
Only this would inspire private investors to spend money on creating new jobs, he added.

Europe's preparations for Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) were in the limelight when the bankers were briefed by Alexander Lamfalussy, president of the European Monetary Institute, the forerunner to the future European central bank.

"There is a clear convergence as far as inflation and long-term rates...but the problem is still in the budget field," Tietmeyer said, adding a lot of effort was still needed to resolve stubborn fiscal and debt challenges.
Countries seeking to be founding members of the single european currency will be judged next year on whether they qualify, based on their economic performance in 1997.
The G10 did not discuss in detail where countries stood on meeting the criteria, he added.
